endings.text: You asked whether the cholera was near and carry back a report, not a promise: news weighed from other towns, a rumour that could not be traced, and the editor's word that Chicago is healthy.
You asked what was new today and carry back a sale: an auction room's first, on South Water Street, this very morning. What will be sold the notice leaves to whoever brings the goods.

One of the two notices fooled you, which is worth knowing too. The Democrat named the papers its cholera news came from; the elixir was signed, dated and sold by the druggist. Read them again over breakfast.
You kept the advertisement. It promises a certain cure, and a promise is all it is: signed by the seller, reported by no editor. A useful thing to know, and you carry it back.
Two papers compared before breakfast and one clipping in your pocket. The morning's lesson travels with it: a report names where its news came from, and an advertisement names who is selling.

evidence.text: In June 1835 Chicago had two weekly papers: the Democrat, published every Wednesday, and the American, established by T. O. Davis on 8 June 1835 and published on Saturday mornings.

evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), the imprint; Andreas vol. 1, the press chapter on Calhoun’s office.
evidence.text: The Democrat’s first issue, 26 November 1833, gives its office as the building on the corner of South Water and Clark streets; John Calhoun printed it there.

evidence.locator: 20 May 1835 (Vol. II No. 5), p. 4, col. 6, the colophon (transcription lines 4177–4180). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: By 20 May 1835 the Democrat’s colophon gives the office as over Messrs. Jones & King’s hardware store, in South Water Street, so the corner is a former office on the scene date.

evidence.locator: 24 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 10), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph headed ‘CHOLERA.’ (transcription lines 1481–1505; extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_24#c003). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: Under the heading CHOLERA the Democrat lays out rumours of the disease in the state: a Springfield paper on the state of health there, the Alton Spectator’s count of about twenty deaths in three weeks with most cases recovering, no mention in the Galenian, and an Ottawa rumour it could not trace. It calls Chicago uncommonly healthy and promises to print the facts if the disease appears.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives a street and a landmark, not a lot. The structure record’s inferred position reads the drawbridge as the 1834 Dearborn Street bridge, so the stop says ‘near the drawbridge’ and claims no front door.
evidence.text: The Chicago American’s office was on Water Street near the drawbridge; this project places it on the south side of South Water Street just east of Dearborn, by the south landing of the Dearborn Street bridge.

evidence.locator: 27 June 1835 (Vol. I No. 4), p. 3, col. 5 (transcription lines 362–365; extracted claim chicago_american_1835_06_27#c011). Transcription-mediated reading: the signature prints ‘FREDERICK THO[…]’, completed from the same druggist’s 20 June notice; the column is crowded and partly illegible.
evidence.text: The American of 27 June 1835 carries an advertisement headed ‘The Cholera El[ixir]’, offering the Fire King’s Specific as a certain preventive and cure of the asphyxiated cholera, signed by Frederick Thomas, druggist, Water Street, and dated Chicago, 24 June 1835.

evidence.locator: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 635, the hotel chapter (builder, corner, proprietors, the 1839 fire); the Chicago Tribune letter of 2 February 1874 transcribed on chicagology_prefire021, for Ira Couch taking the house in 1834. The structure record tremont_house_1 carries both readings.
evidence.text: Alanson Sweet built the first Tremont House, a frame building, in 1833 on the north-west corner of Lake and Dearborn streets. Ira Couch took the house in 1834, and Andreas names the Couch brothers among its keepers before it burned on 27 October 1839.

evidence.locator: 24 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 10), p. 3, col. 3 (transcription lines 2540–2559, interleaved; extracted claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_24#c008). Transcription-mediated reading; the auctioneer’s surname reads MONTGOMERY and his initials are lost. The American’s 27 June copy of the notice is ambiguous between the first and the last day of July, so only the Democrat’s reading is used.
evidence.text: A notice headed ‘[Auction an]d Commission House’ announces a store taken on South Water Street for auction and commission business, its first public sale to be held ‘the 1st day of July’, which is the scene date.

evidence.reasoning: Uses the existing structure records’ scene-date phases and positions, all of which are inferred. The Democrat’s structure keeps its name but has lost the press by May 1835, so the stop speaks of where the paper was printed, not of a press at work on the morning.
evidence.text: The four places are exterior stops in the 1 July 1835 scene. The Democrat’s corner is visited as its former office, the American’s office is placed near the drawbridge, and no interior, front door, keeper on the morning or newsroom is claimed.

opening.text: Chicago prints two weekly papers this summer, and one of them is three weeks old. Choose a question, ride from your lodging to both offices, decide which columns report and which ones sell, and carry one clipping to breakfast. The morning, the ride and the clipping are invented; the printed words are not.

premise: Read both of the town's papers before breakfast, tell a report from an advertisement and keep one useful clipping.
